metadata.title: How Does Claude Build a Due Diligence Checklist?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude uses its own judgment to decide what belongs in a due diligence checklist -- or is doing something narrower. Lands the carry-out that the checklist tailors known workstreams to the deal's sector and type from a written file, and only escalates what it's already tracking.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the dd-checklist skill generates and tracks due diligence checklists tailored to the target's sector, deal type, and complexity; covers major workstreams with request lists, status tracking, and red-flag escalation; used when kicking off diligence, organizing a data room review, or tracking outstanding items. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (a software acquisition's 'customer contracts' request: requested -> received -> reviewed -> flagged) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks whether Claude uses its own judgment to decide what belongs in a due diligence checklist. It doesn't. Liam is here to take you through what the skill actually does, step by step.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'What decides the checklist -- judgment?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'the file', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'the file') is visible on a late frame, fully settled before the beat ends.

beats.narration_text: The natural guess is that Claude sizes up this specific deal and decides, from its own judgment, which risks are worth chasing. But the skill doesn't work that way. It reads the target's sector, deal type, and complexity, then builds the checklist from workstreams the file already defines — request lists, status tracking, red-flag escalation. Hand it a sector the file never lists, and it has no independent research to reach for.

shot.new_visual_element: A deal-judgment figure weighing risks ad hoc, struck through; a sector/type/complexity-to-workstreams procedure card lit instead

production_viz.label: Deal judgment, struck -- sector/type/complexity, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'DEAL JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'SECTOR + TYPE -> WORKSTREAMS' listing three steps: read sector/type/complexity, match workstream templates, build request lists. The judgment side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'sector not listed -- no template' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: What the skill actually does: read the deal's sector, type, and complexity, then generate the workstreams that profile calls for, each with its own request list. Watch the anchor: a software company acquisition. 'Customer contracts' goes out as a request, comes back received, gets reviewed — and one clause, heavy revenue concentration in a single customer, gets flagged as a red flag for the deal team.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a 'customer contracts' request traveling requested -> received -> reviewed -> flagged

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one request, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'REQUESTED', 'RECEIVED', 'REVIEWED', 'FLAGGED'. A single highlighted token 'CUSTOMER CONTRACTS' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting terracotta as it arrives. At the bottom, beside the FLAGGED card, a small note reads 'revenue concentration -- one customer' and the token halts there. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, CONDENSED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: That flag reaches the deal team because the item was on the checklist to begin with — the skill escalates what it's already tracking, it doesn't go looking beyond the list. Ask for that same software acquisition checklist twice, and the workstreams and request items come back identical both times. But ask for a deal type the file never described — say, a mineral rights transfer — and there's nothing tailored to reach for; the checklist stops exactly where SKILL.md does.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, condensed; splits into 'run twice -- same checklist' and 'mineral rights transfer -- no template'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- run twice, or stops there
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 COMPOSITION RETURNS, condensed to a small resting row (RECEIVED / REVIEWED / FLAGGED). It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'RUN TWICE' then 'SAME CHECKLIST' with a checkmark, labelled 'same input, same checklist' (holds); right reads 'MINERAL RIGHTS TRANSFER' then a struck-through 'TAILORED?', labelled 'stops where the file does' (flips).

beats.narration_text: A Claude due diligence checklist isn't independent judgment about a deal's risks — it's a written procedure that tailors known workstreams to the deal's sector and type, and it only flags what it's already tracking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Give me a deal profile — say, a software company acquisition — and run the dd-checklist skill: build the workstreams, the request lists inside each one, and where red-flag escalation would trigger. Then ask for a sector or deal type you've never mentioned supporting, and see whether new workstreams get invented or the checklist stops where the file does. Liam, in for Bear.
